curatorBrief.title: Welcome to Shape Safari!
curatorBrief.intent: Welcome young kindergarten learners to the wonderful world of shapes! Introduce our core goals: finding real-world objects shaped like circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles; identifying and naming these basic 2D shapes; and comparing them by counting straight sides and pointy corners.

objectiveBlocks.objectiveText: Find and touch real objects around the room that match basic shapes

components.title: Shapes All Around Our Room
components.intent: Explore real-world classroom items that match core shapes: a round clock, a square window, a triangular slice of pizza or banner, and a rectangular door. Allow students to tap each item to reveal its matching shape outline and hear clear, friendly spoken descriptions.

components.title: Shape Sorting Trays
components.intent: Present everyday objects (plates, picture frames, party hats, envelopes) one at a time and ask the child to say out loud which shape tray the object belongs to, reinforcing real-world shape application.

components.title: Family Shape Hunt
components.intent: Guide caregivers and students on a playful scavenger hunt around their home or yard to spot, touch, and name real items matching circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles.

objectiveBlocks.objectiveText: Identify and name circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles

components.title: Meet the Shape Family
components.intent: Introduce four fundamental 2D shapes: Circle, Square, Triangle, and Rectangle. Feature bold, colorful illustrations with audio narration clearly pronouncing each shape's name.

components.title: Trace the Shapes
components.intent: Engage fine-motor and visual shape memory by having students trace dotted lines of circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles, reinforcing distinct boundaries and names.

components.title: Say the Shape Name
components.intent: Display drawn shapes one at a time at various orientations and sizes. Have the live tutor prompt the student to say the shape's name out loud into the microphone.

objectiveBlocks.objectiveText: Compare shapes by looking at their straight sides and corners

components.title: Sides and Corners: Straight vs Round
components.intent: Side-by-side visual comparison between a circle (round curve, no straight sides, no corners) and a triangle (three straight sides, three pointy corners), with animated highlights emphasizing where edges meet.

components.title: Count Sides and Corners Aloud
components.intent: The live tutor highlights straight sides and pointy corners on triangles, squares, and rectangles, prompting the child to speak out loud how many sides or corners each shape has.

components.title: Corner and Side Discovery
components.intent: Let students tap vertices and connect line segments on a simple peg grid to construct shapes with 3 straight sides versus 4 straight sides, discovering how sides form corners.

finalAssessment.title: Super Shape Explorer Challenge
finalAssessment.intent: Assess kindergarten understanding across all three objectives: recognizing real-world shapes, correctly naming 2D shapes, and answering simple questions about side and corner counts with spoken or tap responses.

data.title: Super Shape Detective Scavenger Hunt
data.subject: Math
data.overview: Grab your detective hat and search your home for hidden shapes all around you! In this playful hunt, you will touch, trace, and sort everyday treasures to discover the secrets of circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles.
learningObjectives: Identify and name four basic 2D shapes: circle, square, triangle, and rectangle in real-world environments.
Describe shapes by counting and tracing their straight sides and corners.
Distinguish between squares and rectangles based on side lengths.

substitutes: A designated table or floor space
Placing cards directly next to items

steps.title: Make Your Detective Shape Badges
steps.instruction: Work with a grown-up to draw one big shape on each of your 4 cards: draw a circle on one, a square on the second, a triangle on the third, and a rectangle on the fourth.
steps.tip: Draw the shapes large enough to fill most of each card so they are easy to compare with objects you find.

steps.title: Finger-Trace the Side and Corners
steps.instruction: Run your finger along the edges of your cards. Trace the circle to feel how round and smooth it is, then feel the pointy corners and straight lines on the square, rectangle, and triangle.

checkpoint.question: Can you find any corners or straight edges on the circle card?

steps.scienceNote: Circles have one continuous curved line and zero sharp corners (vertices), while polygons have straight edges that meet at corners.

steps.title: Hunt for Round Circles
steps.instruction: Carry your circle badge around the room. Look high and low for 2 or 3 items that roll, spin, or have a round face like your circle card, and place them in your collection basket.
steps.tip: Look in the kitchen or toy bin—jar lids, coasters, and toy wheels make wonderful circles!

steps.title: Hunt for Even Squares
steps.instruction: Search for 2 or 3 objects that have 4 straight sides that are all the exact same length. Line them up beside your square badge.

checkpoint.question: How many equal sides does each square item have?

steps.tip: Square sticky notes, block faces, and small square books are great targets.

steps.title: Hunt for Long Rectangles
steps.instruction: Search for 2 or 3 items that have 4 straight sides and 4 corners, but have 2 sides that are long and 2 sides that are short.
steps.scienceNote: A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 square corners, just like a square, but its opposite sides are equal rather than all four sides being identical.

steps.title: Hunt for Pointy Triangles
steps.instruction: Triangles can be sneaky to find inside! Look for 1 or 2 items that have exactly 3 straight sides and 3 sharp corners. If you cannot find a solid object, look for triangle patterns on rugs, pictures, or folded napkins.

checkpoint.question: Point to each corner of your triangle item one by one. Did you count exactly 3 corners?

steps.tip: Fold a square paper napkin corner-to-corner to create a triangle if you cannot find one in the room!

steps.title: Sort and Group the Evidence
steps.instruction: Lay out all 4 shape badges on the carpet or a large table. Place every item you collected next to its matching shape badge, sorting all your treasures into four shape teams.

checkpoint.question: What do you notice about which shape was the easiest to find around your home?

reflectionPrompts.question: Which shape was the easiest to find in your house, and which shape was the hardest?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Identify and name four basic 2D shapes: circle, square, triangle, and rectangle in real-world environments.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about doors, windows, and boxes—do you see more round edges or straight lines in houses?

reflectionPrompts.question: How can you tell the difference between a square and a rectangle when you hold them side by side?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Distinguish between squares and rectangles based on side lengths.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Look at the sides: are all four sides the same, or are two sides stretched longer?

reflectionPrompts.question: Why do you think things with wheels, like bicycles and toy cars, are shaped like circles instead of squares?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Describe shapes by counting and tracing their straight sides and corners.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Imagine trying to roll a box across the floor versus rolling a ball.

documentationPrompt.instruction: Arrange your sorted items in four groups around your shape badges and take a picture looking down from above.
documentationPrompt.suggestedCaption: I became a Shape Detective today! I found [number] shapes around my home. My favorite shape was the [circle/square/triangle/rectangle] because [reason]!

extensions.title: Shape Builder Challenge
extensions.description: Use pretzel sticks, dry spaghetti, or toothpicks paired with playdough or mini marshmallows to build your own 3D versions of shapes or flat 2D outlines.

extensions.title: Secret Shape Feely Bag
extensions.description: Place one shape object inside a pillowcase. Have a partner reach in without peeking, feel the edges and corners, and guess the shape purely by touch!

safetyNotes: Adult helper recommended throughout the scavenger hunt to ensure child stays away from stairs, hot appliances, and breakable items.
Only gather items that are safe, unbroken, and clean (avoid glass cups, sharp edges, or heavy items).
Watch out for small choking hazards if small craft items or small objects are gathered.

problems.question: Which shape is a circle?
problems.rationale: A circle is completely round with no straight sides or corners. The red shape is round all the way around, making it a circle. Squares and triangles have straight lines and pointy corners.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage young learners to trace the shape in the air with their finger to feel the smooth, curved line of a circle versus the sharp corners of a square or triangle.
successCriteria: Identify a circle from a set of basic geometric shapes
Distinguish curved shapes from shapes with straight sides and corners
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which one belongs in the triangle group?
problems.rationale: A pizza slice has three pointy corners and three sides, so it belongs in the triangle group. The gift box and the window have four straight sides, which puts them in the square group. Counting the sides helps us sort each shape into its matching home!
problems.teachingNote: Have learners trace the edges of each object in the air with their finger. Encourage them to count the three straight sides of the pizza slice aloud to reinforce triangle recognition.
successCriteria: Identify real-world objects that have a triangular shape
Sort everyday objects into categories by their shape
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.statement: A square has four straight sides.
problems.rationale: A square is a special shape that always has four straight sides that are the same length. This statement is true and helps us easily tell squares apart from round shapes like circles. Counting the straight sides is a great way to check if a shape is a square!
problems.teachingNote: Have students use their fingers to trace the four straight sides of a paper square to physically feel the shape's properties.
successCriteria: Identify the number of sides on a square
Recognize straight sides on basic 2D shapes
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: A triangle has three _____.
problems.rationale: A triangle is a flat shape that has three straight lines called sides. Circles and squares are separate shapes, not the parts that make up a triangle.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage learners to trace the three sides of a triangle with their finger while counting 1, 2, 3.
successCriteria: Identify that a triangle is defined by having three sides
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which thing is shaped like a circle?
problems.rationale: A round wall clock has a curved edge with no corners, which makes it a circle. A window is shaped like a square, and a pennant flag is shaped like a triangle. Looking for curved lines helps us spot circles all around our classroom!
problems.teachingNote: Have children trace round items with their fingers to feel the continuous curve without sharp corners or flat sides.
successCriteria: Identify real-world objects that have a circular shape

detectedConstraints.description: The digital screen interface cannot directly verify the physical action of finding and touching real objects around the room, leaving the objective assessed only via depicted objects.
Tasks evaluate counting side/corner attributes and constructing shapes rather than directly comparing two or more shapes.

coverage.summary: The lesson thoroughly teaches basic 2D shapes and provides robust, direct assessment for identifying and naming circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles (obj2). However, mastery inferences are unsupported for obj1 and obj3: finding and touching objects around the room is assessed only indirectly via on-screen representations, and comparison based on sides and corners is tested through component counting and building tasks rather than direct shape comparison.
